title: The unreliable narrator: how to read a storyteller you cannot trust
examples: Who coined the term unreliable narrator?
How do you spot an unreliable narrator?

explain.say: Edgar Allan Poe's 1843 story The Tell-Tale Heart opens with a narrator insisting he is not mad, only nervous, and then calmly describing a murder. The more he insists, the less we believe him. He is an unreliable narrator, a teller whose account we cannot fully trust. The board sorts four kinds.

explain.say: How do we know? The critic Wayne C. Booth, who coined the term in 1961, said the author leaves signals behind the narrator's back. Look at the clues: contradictions, other characters reacting oddly, over-insisting, and gaps where key moments should be. Booth called that hidden author the implied author. Which clue do you notice first when a friend tells a story?

explain.say: Some narrators are not lying at all; they deceive themselves. Ishiguro's butler Stevens cannot admit he loved Miss Kenton. In Ford Madox Ford's The Good Soldier, the narrator calls his tale the saddest story he has ever heard, yet failed to see what happened in front of him for nine years. Why are self-deceivers so moving?

Now a naive narrator: Huck Finn in Mark Twain's 1884 novel. Huck believes helping Jim, who has escaped slavery, is a sin, and decides he will go to hell for it. On the left, Huck's judgement; on the right, ours: his heart is right and his society is wrong. How does Twain use a boy's misunderstanding to judge a whole society?

points: He will go to hell for it

explain.say: And sometimes the narrator simply hides the truth. Spoiler warning: in Agatha Christie's 1926 mystery The Murder of Roger Ackroyd, the narrator turns out to be the killer, and readers felt both cheated and thrilled. Great work. Challenge: retell a fairy tale as the wolf, and plant three clues that he is not telling the truth.

faq.a: A narrator whose account the reader cannot fully trust, because they are naive, self-deceiving, mentally disturbed, biased or lying. The reader must read between the lines to find what really happened.

faq.q: Who coined the term unreliable narrator?
faq.a: The American critic Wayne C. Booth, in his 1961 book The Rhetoric of Fiction. He defined a narrator as unreliable when they do not speak or act in line with the norms of the work.

faq.q: How do you spot an unreliable narrator?
faq.a: Look for contradictions, gaps, over-insistence, strange reactions from other characters, and moments where events seem to mean more than the narrator says. Then ask what the narrator gains by their version.
Booth's term for the sense of the author's values and design that we infer from the whole work, distinct from the narrator. The implied author lets us see past an unreliable narrator.
A narrator, often a child or an innocent, who reports events accurately but misunderstands them, like Huck Finn. The irony lies between what they see and what we understand.

facts: Wayne C. Booth introduced the term unreliable narrator in The Rhetoric of Fiction (1961).
Poe's The Tell-Tale Heart was first published in 1843.
Agatha Christie's The Murder of Roger Ackroyd was published in 1926.
